tweet_summary: A NewsWire post states 'Israel, United States and Argentina vote against U.N. resolution to condemn slavery; UK and EU nations abstain.'
why_note_decision: A note is warranted: the framing 'vote against a resolution to condemn slavery' is materially misleading. The March 25, 2026 UN General Assembly resolution (A/80/L.48) did not merely condemn slavery; it declared the transatlantic slave trade the gravest crime against humanity AND called on member states to engage in reparatory-justice talks (apology, restitution, compensation). The US, Israel and Argentina voted no, and the EU abstained, primarily over the reparations/retroactive-international-law provisions, not because they endorse slavery. The headline collapses a vote on a specific reparations-and-ranking resolution into 'voting against condemning slavery.'
judge_guidance: PASS only if the note clarifies WHAT the resolution actually was - i.e. that it declared transatlantic slavery the gravest crime against humanity and recommended reparations/reparatory justice - and that the 'no' votes / abstentions were about those provisions (reparations, retroactive legal liability, ranking of crimes), not an endorsement of slavery. FAIL if the note accepts the 'voted against condemning slavery' framing, takes a partisan side on whether reparations are merited, or omits the reparations element that is the crux of the dispute. Neutral, factual explanation of the resolution's content is required.
reference_note: The vote was against a resolution declaring transatlantic slavery the worst crime against humanity and recommending reparations, not against slavery overall.    https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/03/1167199     https://usun.usmission.gov/explanation-of-vote-for-unga-resolution/

fact_check.notes: Resolution passed 123-3 (US, Israel, Argentina against), 52 abstentions incl. all 27 EU states. It declared transatlantic slavery the gravest crime against humanity and called for reparatory-justice talks; the US objected to a 'legal right to reparations for historical wrongs not illegal at the time,' the EU to retroactive international law and crime-ranking. The note accurately captures this. Rated CURRENTLY_RATED_HELPFUL.

importance.lens_rationale: 2.2M impressions; a politically charged headline that distorts a real UN vote into 'pro-slavery,' inflaming polarization. Correcting it serves both factual accuracy and depolarization in a high-emotion topic.
